levels.title: Best Fit Line
levels.story: Fenn is staking tomato plants in a straight row. "More water, more tomatoes," Fenn says, "but how many more for each extra litre? If I could draw one straight line through my notes, I could read off a guess for any amount of water."

everyday.scene: A taxi app tells you the fare before you set off. The fare is roughly a starting charge plus a price per kilometre, so a straight line connects the distance to the cost.
everyday.question: How can a computer predict a number, such as a price or a weight, from other numbers?
everyday.answer: It can fit a straight line to past examples and read the prediction off the line. That is linear regression.

lessons.title: A line that predicts a number
text: A line has two settings: the slope, how much y goes up for each step in x, and the intercept, where it crosses when x is zero. The prediction is y = slope x + intercept.

Regression predicts a number, such as kilograms of tomatoes. That differs from classification, which predicts a label such as Plum or Apricot. The table shows five plants: litres a week and kilograms of tomatoes.

terms.meaning: How much the prediction rises for one more step in x.
The prediction when x is zero.

lessons.title: Least squares
text: A residual is the actual value minus the line's prediction. Squaring each residual stops over and under from cancelling, and makes big misses count extra. The best line has the smallest sum of squared residuals. That is called least squares.
The table scores three candidate lines on the five plants. The smaller the sum, the better the fit.

predict.prompt: Which of the three lines fits best?
predict.answer: Line C, y = x + 1, because its sum, 0.11, is the smallest.

lessons.title: Using and misusing a line
text: The least-squares line for these plants has slope 1.03 and intercept 0.89. Its sum of squared residuals is about 0.10, a hair better than line C. At 6 litres it predicts 1.03 x 6 + 0.89 = 7.07 kg.

Be careful past the edge of your data. Nobody watered a plant with 6 litres, so that prediction is a guess about a place you have never looked. A straight line also cannot bend, so it fits curved patterns badly.

fieldNotes.title: Ordinary least squares
fieldNotes.text: Ordinary least squares is the most common way to fit a linear regression line. It chooses the line that makes the sum of squared residuals as small as possible.

fieldNotes.title: Linear models in code
fieldNotes.text: scikit-learn's LinearRegression fits a linear model by minimising the residual sum of squares between observed and predicted values.

summary: You drew a line through five plants, scored it with squared residuals, found the best fit by least squares, and saw why a line should not be trusted past the data.
Fenn ties off the last stake. "A line through the notes, and a number for tomorrow."

mistake.title: Trusting a line far beyond the data it saw
mistake.text: A fitted line describes the range of the examples. Past that range, it is only a guess, and a straight line cannot capture a curve.

levels.title: Yes or No
levels.story: Fenn holds up a melon. "Ripe or not? I don't want a number of kilograms this time. I want a yes or a no, and ideally a chance. 'Eighty percent ripe' is something I can act on."

everyday.scene: A bank's app flags a card payment as 'suspicious' or 'fine'. Behind the flag is a number, like '92% likely a fraud', and a cut-off above which the flag turns on.
everyday.question: How can a model turn facts into a chance, and then into a yes or a no?
everyday.answer: It computes a score, squashes the score into a chance between 0 and 1, and says yes when the chance is above a cut-off. This is logistic regression.

lessons.title: From a score to a chance
text: Like linear regression, logistic regression first computes a score from the features: z = weight x feature + bias. But a score can be any number, and a chance must lie between 0 and 1.
The sigmoid function fixes that: chance = 1 / (1 + e to the power of minus z). A score of 0 gives 0.5. Big negative scores give chances near 0, and big positive scores give chances near 1.

terms.meaning: The S-shaped function that turns any score into a chance.
The weighted sum of the features, before squashing.

lessons.title: Chance to yes or no
text: The model says Yes when the chance is at least 0.5, which is the same as the score being at least 0. The place where the score is exactly 0 is the decision boundary.

For melons, say the score is z = 2x - 5, where x counts warm days. It is zero at x = 2.5, so patches with 3 or more warm days are called ripe. Despite its name, logistic regression is used for classification.

predict.prompt: The score is z = 2x - 5. At what x is the score exactly 0?

references.title: Speech and Language Processing, chapter 5: Logistic Regression

lessons.title: Odds and fitting
text: The score z has a handy meaning: it is the log of the odds. If the chance is 0.8, the odds are 4 to 1, because 0.8 / 0.2 = 4.

The weights are found by picking the ones that make the labelled examples as likely as possible, not by least squares. The 0.5 cut-off can also move. A cautious farmer might demand 0.9 before calling a melon ripe.

fieldNotes.title: Not for numbers
fieldNotes.text: Despite its name, logistic regression models the probability of a yes-or-no outcome. The model itself is not a classifier, but a cutoff on that probability turns it into one.

fieldNotes.title: The S-shaped curve
fieldNotes.text: The logistic function squashes any real number into the range between 0 and 1, which is why it can model probabilities.

summary: You turned a score into a chance with the sigmoid, found where the model switches from No to Yes, and saw how moving the cut-off changes the answers.
Fenn sets the ripe melons on the cart. "A chance I can act on."

mistake.title: Thinking logistic regression predicts a number
mistake.text: It predicts a chance and then a yes or no. The word regression is a historical name.
